title: Complex Noun Phrases
subtitle: C1 writing and speech often packs a lot of information into a single noun phrase instead of spreading it across several short sentences. Four tools make this po…
objectives: Understand and use: Multiple modifiers — stacking adjectives, participles, and prepositional phrases before and after a noun.

Understand and use: Nominalization — turning a verb or adjective into a noun (often with -tion, -ment, -ness, -ity) to make writing more compact, formal and objective. This is very common in academic and journalistic style.
Understand and use: Expanded relative clauses — relative clauses with extra detail, sometimes non-defining (set off by commas) and stacked with other modifiers.
Understand and use: Reduced relative clauses — relative clauses shortened by dropping the relative pronoun and auxiliary, using a participle instead.

content.intro: C1 writing and speech often packs a lot of information into a single noun phrase instead of spreading it across several short sentences. Four tools make this possible:

rules.heading: a) Multiple modifiers — stacking adjectives, participles, and prepositional phrases before and after a noun.
rules.body: a rapidly growing, community-led initiative to reduce plastic waste

rules.heading: b) Nominalization — turning a verb or adjective into a noun (often with -tion, -ment, -ness, -ity) to make writing more compact, formal and objective. This is very common in academic and journalistic style.
rules.body:
They decided to reduce costs. → Their decision to reduce costs...

The company failed unexpectedly. → The company's unexpected failure...

rules.heading: c) Expanded relative clauses — relative clauses with extra detail, sometimes non-defining (set off by commas) and stacked with other modifiers.
rules.body: The report, which was released last Friday and which contradicts earlier findings, sparked controversy.

rules.heading: d) Reduced relative clauses — relative clauses shortened by dropping the relative pronoun and auxiliary, using a participle instead.
rules.body:
The man who is standing by the door → The man standing by the door

The results that were published last year → The results published last year

Reduced relative clauses use the -ing form for active meaning (the man standing...) and the past participle for passive meaning (the results published...). They make sentences more compact and are especially common in written and journalistic English.

examples: The recently renovated, award-winning museum attracts thousands of visitors a year.
Her decision to resign surprised everyone on the board.
The rapid deterioration of the local ecosystem alarmed environmentalists.
The proposal, which had been debated for months, was finally rejected.
The scientist leading the research presented her findings yesterday.
Documents found at the scene confirmed the timeline of events.
The government's growing concern about inflation shaped its policy.
A heavily criticized, poorly funded healthcare system struggled to cope.
The book, written during the author's exile, became an instant classic.
Employees affected by the layoffs will receive severance packages.
The committee's reluctance to act delayed the reforms significantly.
The bridge connecting the two islands took a decade to build.

commonMistakes.wrong: The man who standing by the door is my uncle.
commonMistakes.right: The man standing by the door is my uncle.
commonMistakes.why: A reduced relative clause drops both the relative pronoun ("who") and the auxiliary ("is") — keep only the participle.

commonMistakes.wrong: The report wrote last year was inaccurate.
commonMistakes.right: The report written last year was inaccurate.
commonMistakes.why: For a passive meaning, use the past participle (written), not the past simple (wrote).

commonMistakes.wrong: His decide to leave shocked the team.
commonMistakes.right: His decision to leave shocked the team.
commonMistakes.why: Nominalization requires the noun form of the verb ("decision"), not the bare verb.

commonMistakes.wrong: The company success unexpected surprised analysts.
commonMistakes.right: The company's unexpected success surprised analysts.
commonMistakes.why: Word order matters — possessive + adjective + noun, not noun + adjective in that order.

commonMistakes.wrong: The employees affecting by the cuts were notified.
commonMistakes.right: The employees affected by the cuts were notified.
commonMistakes.why: "Affected" (past participle, passive meaning: they were affected) is needed, not "affecting" (active meaning).

exercises.title: Guided Production
exercises.instructions: Write your own sentence. There's no single correct answer — a model answer is shown for comparison after you submit.

items.prompt: Write one sentence with a reduced relative clause describing a person (using -ing).
items.modelAnswer: The woman waiting at the bus stop looked exactly like my cousin.

items.prompt: Write one sentence with a reduced relative clause describing an object (using a past participle).
items.modelAnswer: The letter delivered this morning changed everything.

items.prompt: Write one sentence using nominalization to describe a decision or change in your life.
items.modelAnswer: My decision to change careers was the best choice I've ever made.

items.prompt: Write one sentence with a noun phrase that stacks at least two modifiers before the noun.
items.modelAnswer: A quietly confident, highly experienced negotiator led the talks.

summary: a) Multiple modifiers — stacking adjectives, participles, and prepositional phrases before and after a noun.

b) Nominalization — turning a verb or adjective into a noun (often with -tion, -ment, -ness, -ity) to make writing more compact, formal and objective. This is very common in academic and journalistic style.
c) Expanded relative clauses — relative clauses with extra detail, sometimes non-defining (set off by commas) and stacked with other modifiers.
d) Reduced relative clauses — relative clauses shortened by dropping the relative pronoun and auxiliary, using a participle instead.
